papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — US registry epidemiology of a past pandemic wave — useful context for how arrests and resuscitation workload shift during a high-consequence infectious event, not for everyday practice.
papers.design: Retrospective observational cohort
papers.n: 4,423 EMS encounters for OHCA, 2016–2022, ~537,500 population
papers.finding: OHCA incidence increased across all seasons (peak fall 2020); termination-of-resuscitation rate 56.6% → 61.2% (P=.01); scene times 24.4 → 26.1 minutes (P=.04) with transport times unchanged
papers.caveat: Retrospective ecological comparison of periods with no adjustment for case mix
papers.shortTitle: More arrests, more TORs during the pandemic years
papers.learningGoal: Understand how pandemic-era pressures reshaped out-of-hospital cardiac arrest incidence and resuscitation decision making.

papers.title: More Than a Tobacco Problem: Cigarette Smoking as a Marker of Poorer Cardiovascular Health Among Emergency Medical Services Clinicians
papers.summary: A US cross-sectional survey analysis of nationally certified EMS clinicians found current smokers had poorer cardiovascular health beyond the tobacco exposure itself — lower adjusted Life's Essential 7 scores (β −6.02) and lower odds of ideal cardiovascular health (aOR 0.37) than never smokers.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A US certified-clinician survey, but workforce cardiovascular health is the same occupational question here, and smoking as a marker of broader risk clusters is relevant to any service's wellbeing programme.
papers.design: Cross-sectional secondary analysis of a voluntary recertification survey
papers.n: 7,703 EMTs, advanced EMTs and paramedics with complete data (of 36,436 respondents)
papers.finding: Current smokers (6.0%) had adjusted mLE7 score −6.02 (95% CI −7.63 to −4.41) and aOR 0.37 for ideal cardiovascular health versus never smokers; former smokers intermediate (aOR 0.73)
papers.caveat: Voluntary self-reported survey data with selection and recall bias
papers.shortTitle: Smoking flags wider heart risk in EMS staff
papers.learningGoal: Understand how smoking signals broader cardiovascular risk in the paramedic workforce and what that means for my own wellbeing.

papers.title: Debriefing in prehospital simulation-based education: a scoping review of ambulance nurse and paramedic literature
papers.summary: A scoping review of 18 studies (2005–2025) on debriefing after prehospital simulation for practising paramedics and ambulance nurses found debriefing was associated with better technical performance, communication and teamwork, but how it was run and reported varied widely.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Simulation debriefing is standard in Australian services' training, so the gap this review names — inconsistent structure, facilitation and outcome reporting — is directly actionable for clinical education units here.
papers.design: Scoping review (Arksey and O'Malley framework, PRISMA-ScR)
papers.n: 18 studies from 974 records, mostly US and quantitative
papers.finding: Guided debriefing in 15 studies and tool/technology-assisted in 3; debriefing associated with improvements in technical performance, communication, teamwork, clinical reasoning and reflective practice, with inconsistent reporting of facilitation, structure and outcomes
papers.caveat: Mostly self-reported educational outcomes, so debriefing's specific contribution can't be separated from simulation itself
papers.shortTitle: Debriefing works, but nobody reports it the same way
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my debriefing practice after simulation and clinical cases to improve teamwork and reflective judgement.

papers.title: Impact of heat alerts on mortality and emergency ambulance dispatches in Japan
papers.summary: A Japanese time-series study matching heat-alert days with similar-heat non-alert days across 47 prefectures found emergency ambulance dispatches rose on alert days — all-cause +3.11% and heatstroke +31.1% — with no significant mortality difference.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Japan's heat-alert system differs from Australian heatwave arrangements, but the operational point — alerts don't hold down ambulance demand on extreme days, and may lift it via awareness — lands squarely on Australian summer surge planning.
papers.design: National daily time-series analysis with matched days and conditional Poisson regression
papers.n: 2,715 heat-alert days 2020–2023, 1,310 matched pairs (2,620 observation days)
papers.finding: Emergency ambulance dispatches on heat-alert days rose all-cause by 3.11% (95% CI 1.74–4.50), genitourinary by 5.82% and heatstroke by 31.1% (95% CI 21.2–41.8); no significant mortality association
papers.caveat: Matching can't separate any alert effect from heightened public awareness or diagnostic shifts, and mortality data ended in 2022
papers.shortTitle: Heat-alert days bring more ambulance dispatches, not fewer
papers.learningGoal: Understand how public heat alerts shape ambulance demand and preparedness during extreme heat events.

papers.title: Terminology Without Consensus: A Thematic Analysis of Nomenclature Choice and Program Structure Among Expanded EMS Programs in a Single State
papers.summary: A US qualitative study interviewing 23 expanded-EMS programs in Ohio found inconsistent use and interpretation of mobile integrated health and community paramedicine terminology, with one in four programs using alternative names.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A US tiered-response and community paramedicine model that only some Australian services run, but the naming-and-identity confusion it documents mirrors debates wherever ambulance services stretch beyond transport.
papers.design: Qualitative thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews
papers.n: 23 of 58 identified expanded-EMS programs in Ohio
papers.finding: Inconsistent use and interpretation of MIH, CP and MIH-CP terms; 1 in 4 programs used alternative terminology (e.g. neighbourhood paramedic, EMS outreach), attributed to variable definitions and limited stakeholder understanding
papers.caveat: Single US state with 23 of 58 programs participating — selection and generalisability limits
papers.shortTitle: Community paramedicine programs can't agree on names
papers.learningGoal: Understand how inconsistent terminology shapes how community paramedicine programs are understood and integrated in Australian settings.

papers.title: Comparing flipped classroom and lecture-based education on clinical competency in electrocardiogram interpretation among prehospital emergency personnel
papers.summary: An Iranian quasi-experimental pre-post study comparing flipped-classroom with lecture-based teaching found the flipped group had significantly higher ECG interpretation competency scores at two weeks and one month after training among prehospital emergency personnel.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Done with Iranian prehospital personnel in a different training system, but flipped-classroom design is a live question for Australian paramedic education and ECG competency is universal.
papers.design: Quasi-experimental interventional study with pretest-posttest design
papers.n: Prehospital emergency personnel in Iran, 2025 (sample size not reported in abstract)
papers.finding: Flipped-classroom group scored significantly higher at two weeks (mean 6.84, p=0.002) and one month after intervention; groups were equivalent at baseline (p=0.10)
papers.caveat: Quasi-experimental pre-post design with no long-term follow-up and sample details incomplete in the abstract
papers.shortTitle: Flipped classroom beats lectures for ECG skills
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my ECG interpretation skills through active, self-directed learning rather than passive formats.

papers.title: Prehospital Trauma Compendium: Prehospital Management of Pediatric Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Circulatory Arrest – A Joint Position Statement and Resource Document of NAEMSP, ACS-COT, ACEP, and AAP
papers.summary: A US joint position statement and resource document from NAEMSP, ACS-COT, ACEP and AAP updates guidance on withholding or discontinuing resuscitation in paediatric traumatic out-of-hospital circulatory arrest, prioritising reversible causes, rapid haemorrhage control, least-invasive airway care and transport to a trauma centre when safe and appropriate.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Every intervention it recommends — haemorrhage control, least-invasive airway care, chest decompression for suspected tension pneumothorax — is a core Australian paramedic skill; chest decompression is carried by most services but not all, so a couple will still need local guidance on the specifics. The withholding/termination framing aligns with how Australian major-trauma practice treats these cases.
papers.design: Joint position statement and resource document
papers.n: Not applicable (guidance document)
papers.finding: Recommendations: promptly identify children who may benefit from trauma-centre transport; treat reversible causes with direct pressure, wound packing and tourniquets, least-invasive airway management, and chest decompression only if thoracic trauma is suspected (no empiric bilateral decompression); compressions and ventilations have a larger role in paediatric than adult traumatic arrest.
papers.caveat: US consensus guidance, not an Australian guideline — withholding and termination decisions still follow local CPGs.
papers.shortTitle: Updated paediatric traumatic arrest position statement
papers.learningGoal: Refine my judgement on identifying children with traumatic arrest who may benefit from rapid haemorrhage control and trauma-centre transport.

papers.title: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrests due to foreign body airway obstruction: A CanROC registry, retrospective cohort study
papers.summary: A Canadian CanROC registry cohort of 105,178 EMS-treated out-of-hospital cardiac arrests (2005–2023) found 1,106 (1.1%) were obviously foreign-body-airway-obstruction-related: prehospital ROSC was far more frequent than in presumed cardiac arrests (62.7% vs 37.8%) but survival to discharge was similar (10.6% vs 9.0%).
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — A Canadian paramedic-model registry answering a question Australian crews face on every choking arrest. Bystander presence and shorter EMS response times drove outcomes — both central to how Australian systems are built, and the same arrest is managed the same way here.
papers.design: Retrospective registry cohort (CanROC, 2005–2023)
papers.n: 105,178 EMS-treated OHCAs, of which 1,106 obviously FBAO-related
papers.finding: FBAO-related arrests achieved prehospital ROSC more often than presumed cardiac arrests (62.7% vs 37.8%, OR 2.77) but survival to discharge did not differ (10.6% vs 9.0%, p=0.094); within FBAO arrests, survival was 18.1% with prehospital ROSC and 0.8% without, and was associated with younger age (aOR 0.76 per decade), shockable rhythm (aOR 4.76) and shorter EMS response time (aOR 0.81 per minute).
papers.caveat: Exploratory retrospective design, and 'obviously FBAO-related' classification depends on registry coding rather than verified cause of arrest.
papers.shortTitle: Choking arrests: ROSC common, survival still poor
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my recognition of airway obstruction as the reversible cause in cardiac arrest and prioritise early airway clearance.

papers.title: Management of Traumatic Pneumothorax in the Emergency Department: A Two‐Centre Retrospective Cohort Study
papers.summary: An Australian two-centre retrospective cohort of 339 ED patients with traumatic pneumothorax found two-thirds were managed conservatively before leaving the ED, and of the 50 who arrived after a prehospital pleural intervention, 27 had chest drains inserted to formalise finger thoracostomy or needle decompression.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — The endpoints are in-hospital, but the prehospital pleural-intervention subgroup speaks directly to how prehospital needle decompression and finger thoracostomy hold up downstream — a skill most Australian services carry and some don't, so the findings inform practice unevenly across the country.
papers.design: Two-centre retrospective cohort
papers.n: 339 patients aged 14 and over with traumatic pneumothorax
papers.finding: 231 patients (68.1%) were initially managed without drainage; pneumothorax size >35 mm (aOR 41.0, 95% CI 16.4–102) and haemothorax (aOR 6.3, 95% CI 2.5–15.8) predicted ED-initiated drainage; 22.8% of drained patients had a recorded complication and in-hospital mortality was 5.6%.
papers.caveat: Retrospective design at only two EDs, and the prehospital pleural-intervention subgroup is small (n=50).
papers.shortTitle: Traumatic pneumothorax: most EDs don't drain early
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my judgement on when conservative management of traumatic pneumothorax is appropriate after prehospital pleural intervention.

papers.title: Barriers and Enablers of Trauma Triage Tool Implementation in Ireland: A Qualitative Study of First Responders
papers.summary: An Irish study protocol describes a qualitative project using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research to explore barriers and enablers to using the HSE trauma triage tool among up to 30 Dublin Fire Brigade paramedics, advanced paramedics, EMTs, firefighters and managers.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — It sits inside an Irish trauma-system rollout, but trauma triage tools guide major-trauma destination decisions across Australian services, and the implementation friction it targets — time pressure, limited training, resource limits, reluctance to change — is the same here.
papers.design: Qualitative study protocol (phenomenological, CFIR framework)
papers.n: Up to 30 Dublin Fire Brigade responders and managers
papers.finding: Protocol only — semi-structured interviews and focus groups are underway, with results intended to inform Irish trauma triage implementation strategy.
papers.caveat: No findings yet — this is the study protocol, results will come later.
papers.shortTitle: Studying barriers to trauma triage tool use
papers.learningGoal: Understand the system barriers that shape trauma triage tool use in prehospital practice.

papers.title: Oral health behaviours and shift work barriers among Hungarian EMS personnel: a cross-sectional study
papers.summary: A Hungarian nationwide cross-sectional survey of 1,061 National Ambulance Service staff found over half (54.9%) reported current or recent dental or oral problems, and on-duty hygiene-kit availability was strongly associated with daily on-shift brushing (85% vs 21%) among 24-hour shift workers.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — The 24-hour shift patterns mirror Australian ambulance rosters and the fix it points to — enabling on-duty hygiene and routine care — is an organisational one any service could adopt, but oral health is a small slice of workforce wellbeing and the study is self-reported survey data from a single national system.
papers.design: Nationwide cross-sectional online survey
papers.n: 1,061 Hungarian National Ambulance Service staff
papers.finding: 54.9% reported current or recent dental/oral problems, 20% had no dental check-up in two years, and hygiene-kit availability was strongly associated with daily or more frequent on-duty brushing among 24-hour staff (85% vs 21%); 88–90% were willing to undergo workplace screening.
papers.caveat: Self-reported cross-sectional survey — associations, not causation, and no outcome follow-up.
papers.shortTitle: Shift work is rough on paramedics' teeth
papers.learningGoal: Understand how shift work and workplace hygiene-kit access shape oral health for Australian paramedics.

papers.title: Prehospital tranexamic acid in trauma and traumatic brain injury: a systematic review with meta-analysis of randomized comparative evidence
papers.summary: A systematic review of randomised evidence, authored in Saudi Arabia, pooled three trials of prehospital TXA in trauma and found lower 28–30-day mortality (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.68–0.95) without a significant rise in thromboembolic events or seizures.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — TXA is part of standard Australian prehospital trauma care, so this pooled RCT evidence speaks directly to practice rather than a foreign model.
papers.design: Systematic review with meta-analysis restricted to randomised trials (Cochrane RoB2)
papers.n: 21 reports; 3 randomised trials pooled for mortality (PATCH-Trauma, STAAMP, ROC-TXA)
papers.finding: Lower 28–30-day mortality with prehospital TXA (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.68–0.95); TBI mortality (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.64–1.20) and in-hospital mortality came from single trials; no statistically significant increase in thromboembolic events or seizures.
papers.caveat: The mortality pool rests on three trials, and the TBI and in-hospital estimates are single-study; thromboembolic point estimates need watching.
papers.shortTitle: Prehospital TXA lowers mortality in bleeding trauma
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the benefits and thromboembolic risks of prehospital tranexamic acid for bleeding trauma and head injury in my practice.

papers.title: Survival after out of hospital cardiac arrest in relation to AED usage in a multi response system including AED equipped drones
papers.summary: A Swedish registry cohort of 9,413 OHCAs in Västra Götaland found bystander-attached AEDs were associated with the highest 30-day survival (28% vs 9.0% when EMS attached first, OR 2.25), pointing to earlier defibrillation as the key lever.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Bystander defibrillation is a universal weak point in the OHCA chain; the message that earlier community access beats crew arrival applies to every Australian response system.
papers.design: Registry-based cohort study (EMS, dispatch and registry linkage)
papers.finding: EMS attached the first AED in 72% of cases; 30-day survival was 28% with bystander attachment vs 9.0% EMS, 8.7% on-duty first responders and 8.6% community first responders; bystander attachment associated with higher 30-day survival (OR 2.25, 95% CI 1.77–2.85), rising to 62% in witnessed shockable arrests.
papers.caveat: Observational — bystander attachment likely flags arrests recognised and treated earlier, so attribution to the responder alone isn't possible.
papers.shortTitle: Bystander-attached AEDs linked with best OHCA survival
papers.learningGoal: Understand how community AED access and drone-delivered defibrillation shape early bystander response in cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Community First Responder Activation Reduces the Negative Impact of AED Distance on Bystander Defibrillation After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
papers.summary: A Danish registry study of 5,753 OHCAs found HeartRunner community-first-responder activation was associated with more bystander defibrillation at every AED distance (TMLE +6.1 pp) and a modest 1.8-point gain in 30-day survival.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Community first responder apps are a model several Australian systems already use or are trialling; the finding that alerts offset AED distance matters for local AED mapping and CFR footprint.
papers.design: Registry linkage cohort (cardiac arrest registry, AED network, app data) with TMLE
papers.n: 5,753 OHCAs eligible for activation, 2017–2021
papers.finding: Activation (41% of cases) predicted bystander defibrillation of 9.6% vs 5.5% at 389 m and 13.0% vs 4.8% at 1,183 m; TMLE estimated +6.1 pp bystander defibrillation (95% CI 4.5–7.8) and +1.8 pp 30-day survival (95% CI 0.1–3.6).
papers.caveat: The survival gain is small with a lower confidence bound near zero, and activation was not randomised.
papers.shortTitle: First responder alerts linked to more defibrillation
papers.learningGoal: Understand how community first responder systems influence bystander defibrillation rates across Australian communities.

papers.title: A Mobile Application Improves Paramedic Performance in Simulated Trauma Care: A Crossover Randomized Controlled Trial
papers.summary: A US crossover RCT found paramedic pairs using a mobile app with protocols, decision-support tools and procedure videos completed all critical actions in simulated trauma far more often than with standard practice (35.4% vs 6.3%).
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Decision-support apps sit on top of clinical practice every Australian crew already carries; the transferable question is integration with existing app-based guidelines, not the technology itself.
papers.design: Crossover randomised controlled trial, high-fidelity simulation
papers.n: 48 paramedic pairs analysed (112 recruited), adult and paediatric trauma scenarios
papers.finding: 35.4% of app-supported scenarios met all critical actions vs 6.3% without (adjusted OR 8.28, 95% CI 2.21–31.09); paediatric completion 30.4% vs 0%; users rated the app practical and valuable.
papers.caveat: Simulated scenarios rather than patient outcomes, at a single US agency.
papers.shortTitle: Mobile app lifts simulated trauma performance
papers.learningGoal: Build my judgement on integrating mobile decision-support tools into trauma assessment for adults and children.

papers.title: Cost-effectiveness of paramedic-administered prehospital thrombolysis for ST elevation myocardial infarction
papers.summary: An Australian microsimulation of the Queensland prehospital thrombolysis program estimated paramedic-administered STEMI thrombolysis costs AUD 16,750 per QALY gained, concluding it is value for money.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Australian research on a program paramedics deliver; the cost-per-QALY framing is directly useful for service planning and funding arguments anywhere long PCI transfer times exist.
papers.design: Decision-analytic microsimulation model (health-provider perspective, lifetime horizon)
papers.n: Modelled cohort from all QAS STEMI patients receiving prehospital thrombolysis, 2022–2024
papers.finding: AUD 16,750 per QALY gained (95% uncertainty range 15,477–18,423), equivalent to USD 11,725; results robust in sensitivity analysis.
papers.caveat: A model with a hypothetical counterfactual comparator rather than a randomised comparison, and long-term inputs drawn from published literature.
papers.shortTitle: Prehospital STEMI thrombolysis is value for money
papers.learningGoal: Understand the cost-effectiveness considerations underpinning prehospital thrombolysis for STEMI in Australian practice.

papers.title: Five-Year Experience with Automated Head Up Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation for Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
papers.summary: A five-year US registry of 3,709 OHCAs treated with automated head-up CPR (head/thorax positioning plus active compression–decompression and an impedance threshold device) reported 10.5% survival to discharge with favourable neurology, 91% of survivors at CPC 1.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Head-up CPR devices and active compression–decompression aren't standard Australian ambulance equipment — a large real-world dataset from a paramedic-model system, but adoption here would need equipment and guideline change.
papers.design: Prospective observational multicentre registry study
papers.n: 3,709 adults with non-traumatic OHCA across 10 US EMS agencies serving 1.5 million people
papers.finding: ROSC 29.5%, survival to discharge 13.1%, favourable neurological survival 10.5%; shockable rhythm 33.9% favourable survival vs 2.0% asystole; 91% of the 391 survivors had CPC 1.
papers.caveat: No concurrent control group — an observational registry cannot isolate the effect of head-up CPR from concurrent care changes.
papers.shortTitle: Five years of automated head-up CPR outcomes
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the benefits and limitations of automated head-up CPR in my management of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Early Prehospital Prediction of Neurological Outcome After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Derivation and External Validation of the MIRA-29 Score
papers.summary: A French derivation-and-validation study built the MIRA-29 score from five prehospital variables and externally validated it on 82,696 registry patients, identifying poor neurological outcome with 0.99 specificity.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — The variables (low-flow time, shock count, adrenaline dose, arrest site) are collected by paramedics everywhere, but the score grew out of a physician-staffed French system and would need local validation before touching termination-of-resuscitation decisions.
papers.design: Prospective derivation cohort with external registry validation
papers.n: 1,099 derivation patients plus 82,696 external validation patients
papers.finding: Low-flow duration, shock count, adrenaline dose and arrest site predicted neurological outcome; precision 0.86 and recall 0.88 in external validation, specificity for poor outcome 0.99; age was not retained in the final model.
papers.caveat: Derived and validated in a physician-staffed French system, and highly accurate poor-outcome flags raise futility-decision questions that discrimination statistics alone don't answer.
papers.shortTitle: MIRA-29: early prehospital prognosis after arrest
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my judgement on using early prehospital prognostic factors when considering futility after cardiac arrest.

papers.title: RescQTM: One-year implementation and feasibility results of a digitally enabled support pathway for bystanders of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
papers.summary: A one-year UK service evaluation in Essex found the RescQ digital bystander support pathway feasible, with 50.9% of eligible OHCA incidents captured and 96.2% of registered adult bystanders accessing the resources.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Bystander psychological support after cardiac arrest is an emerging expectation for Australian services too, and the pathway is cheap, digital-first and doesn't depend on the UK system's structure.
papers.design: Prospective one-year regional service evaluation
papers.n: 432 eligible OHCA incidents; 260 adult bystanders registered
papers.finding: Incident-level capture 50.9%; 96.2% of registered adults accessed digital resources at least once; ~10% self-referred for liaison officer support; 10.1% of identified bystanders were under 18; EMS clinicians rated it acceptable.
papers.caveat: Single-region service evaluation with capture under 51% and a small clinician survey (25 respondents).
papers.shortTitle: Digital support pathway for OHCA bystanders feasible
papers.learningGoal: Understand how digital bystander support pathways can strengthen community response to out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Prehospital Resource Utilization After Video-Assisted Versus Telephone-Only Emergency Calls: A Post Hoc Analysis of the CAM-VISION Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial
papers.summary: A post hoc analysis of 18,745 calls from the Danish CAM-VISION cluster-randomised trial found video-assisted emergency calls produced no statistically significant reduction in prehospital resource use, though point estimates consistently favoured video.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Video triage on emergency calls is being trialled in Australian dispatch centres, and this is the first complete-pathway look at whether it actually saves resources.
papers.design: Post hoc analysis of a cluster-randomised trial
papers.n: 18,745 emergency calls (8,124 video, 10,621 telephone-only)
papers.finding: Initial dispatch 69.4% vs 73.9% (risk difference −4.5 pp, 95% CI −10.0 to 1.0); cumulative unit time −1.5 min (95% CI −6.2 to 3.1); no outcome reached statistical significance and later dispatch didn't offset the difference.
papers.caveat: Post hoc analysis not powered for resource outcomes, and the confidence intervals don't exclude meaningful differences.
papers.shortTitle: Video calls showed no clear resource savings
papers.learningGoal: Understand how video-assisted emergency calls shape dispatch decisions and prehospital resource use across systems.

papers.title: Survival after neonatal chest compressions at birth: Temporal trends and prognostic factors in a population-based cohort, Queensland, Australia
papers.summary: An Australian population cohort of 3,077 Queensland infants who received chest compressions at birth found 89.0% survived to 28 days, with survival improving from 82% in 2008 to 89% in 2024.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Australian data on a resuscitation paramedics perform at field births, but the cohort is dominated by in-hospital births, so it informs context and counselling more than on-road technique.
papers.design: Retrospective population-based cohort (perinatal data collection)
papers.n: 3,077 liveborn chest-compression recipients, Queensland 2008–2024
papers.finding: 70.5% established regular breathing within 60 minutes and 89.0% survived to 28 days; adjusted survival odds fell with gestational age (aOR 0.17 under 28 weeks), though the term vs moderate-preterm gap attenuated after adjusting for cord pH or adrenaline.
papers.caveat: Administrative data lack compression indications and resuscitation quality measures.
papers.shortTitle: Neonatal chest compressions: most survive a month
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my judgement on prognostic factors influencing newborn survival after birth compressions.

papers.title: Epidemiology, outcomes, and associated factors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in Zhejiang, China: a province-wide registry study
papers.summary: A Chinese province-wide registry study of 17,646 EMS-treated OHCAs in Zhejiang found 3.0% survived to 30 days, with bystander CPR in 47.7% and bystander AED use just 1.8%.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A very different community-response system — the low bystander rates frame how much headroom community response still has, including in Australian systems with similar weak links.
papers.design: Retrospective analysis of a prospective Utstein-style province-wide EMS registry
papers.n: 17,646 EMS-treated adult medical OHCAs, 2024–2025
papers.finding: 30-day survival 3.0%, favourable neurological outcome 2.0%; bystander CPR 47.7%, dispatcher-assisted CPR 20.0%, bystander AED use 1.8%; shockable rhythm the strongest factor for survival and neurological recovery; survival declined with longer EMS response times.
papers.caveat: Retrospective registry data from a community-response system far weaker than Australia's, limiting direct comparison.
papers.shortTitle: Chinese OHCA registry: low survival, low AED use
papers.learningGoal: Recognise the system factors that drive bystander CPR and AED use in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Cardiac cause attribution in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: linkage of a provincial resuscitation registry with the death-registration system in Zhejiang, China
papers.summary: A Chinese registry–death-registration linkage study in Zhejiang showed cardiac cause attribution in OHCA ranged from 20.7% to 42.3% depending on attribution rules and eligibility definitions used.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A registry-methods question that matters to how OHCA epidemiology is counted and compared, less to the road — useful when reading any 'proportion cardiac' claim.
papers.design: Retrospective registry linkage study (bootstrap cluster CIs)
papers.n: 55,720 registry records; 11,427-record linked-death cohort
papers.finding: Cardiac attribution estimates ranged from 20.74% to 42.32% across the definition matrix; in paired records, registry-recorded cardiac attribution was 22.70% vs 27.82% under a broader rule (difference 5.12 pp, 95% CI 0.96–8.51).
papers.caveat: Three-quarters of death-query outcomes were unknown because of identification-document barriers.
papers.shortTitle: OHCA cause attribution shifts with definitions
papers.learningGoal: Recognise how differing cardiac cause attribution definitions shape reported outcomes and epidemiology of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

papers.title: A Lighter Approach to Language Access: Virtual Interpreter Utilization in Emergency Medical Services (EMS)
papers.summary: A US pre-post cohort found issuing EMS clinicians lightweight smartphones (in place of heavy laptops) tripled virtual interpreter use, from 0.19 to 0.57 requests per 100 encounters.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Language barriers are a real problem on Australian crews, and the finding suggests device ergonomics and workflow, not clinician willingness, are the bottleneck.
papers.design: Retrospective pre-post observational cohort
papers.n: 430 interpreter requests across pre- and post-implementation periods
papers.finding: Requests rose from 104 (0.19 per 100 encounters) to 326 (0.57 per 100) after agency-issued smartphones (RR 3.04, 95% CI 2.44–3.79); audio requests tripled; most requested languages were Spanish (36%), Somali (34%) and Arabic (10%).
papers.caveat: Pre-post design — other workflow changes could contribute, and there are no patient outcome data.
papers.shortTitle: Clinician smartphones linked to tripled interpreter use
papers.learningGoal: Understand how portable technology shapes my use of interpreter services for patients with limited English proficiency.

papers.title: Rescue and extrication characteristics associated with morbidity and mortality following road traffic collisions: a scoping review
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: An international scoping review mapped the rescue and extrication literature after road traffic collisions and found fragmented definitions, inconsistent time intervals and heterogeneous outcomes, with no clear effectiveness evidence for any extrication approach.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Extrication decisions are made on Australian roads every shift alongside fire and rescue crews; the review's finding that the evidence base can't settle self-extrication vs rapid extrication is directly relevant to those joint decisions.
papers.design: Scoping review
papers.n: Not reported
papers.finding: Mapped rescue characteristics studied against morbidity, mortality and physiological deterioration; found inconsistent definitions of entrapment, extrication method and time, and heterogenous outcome reporting limiting synthesis and system-level learning.
papers.caveat: A scoping review maps the evidence without evaluating whether any extrication approach works.
papers.shortTitle: Extrication after road collisions: an evidence map
papers.learningGoal: Understand how inconsistent definitions of entrapment and extrication affect patient outcomes and system-level learning.

papers.title: Prehospital Triage and Transport During Mass Casualty Incidents and Disasters
papers.journal: The Surgical Clinics of North America
papers.summary: A US systems review of mass-casualty prehospital triage and transport promotes SALT as the national triage standard, with casualty collection points, ambulance exchange points and incident-command-led transport by a designated transport officer.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A US tiered MCI framework — Australia runs different national triage tools and command structures, so treat this as a systems comparison for anyone working MCI policy or exercises.
papers.design: Narrative clinical review
papers.n: Not reported
papers.finding: Sets out early recognition, resource escalation and dynamic primary/secondary/tertiary triage with retriage, casualty collection and ambulance exchange points, and Incident Command System–structured triage-driven transport.
papers.caveat: A narrative US review reflecting the American MCI framework, not a systematic synthesis of evidence.
papers.shortTitle: A US systems approach to MCI triage
papers.learningGoal: Understand how dynamic retriage and incident command structures shape triage and transport decisions in mass casualty incidents.

papers.title: Factors influencing willingness to perform cardiopulmonary resuscitation and use an automated external defibrillator: a convergent parallel mixed-methods study
papers.summary: A Malaysian mixed-methods study of 449 community members trained in CPR found self-efficacy the strongest predictor of willingness to perform CPR and use an AED, with attitude and perceived norms contributing far less.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — The psychological levers behind bystander action are universal, though community norms and training contexts differ from Australia's — useful for anyone designing CPR awareness programs.
papers.design: Convergent parallel mixed-methods study (SEM plus thematic interviews)
papers.n: 449 survey participants and 10 stakeholder interviews
papers.finding: Self-efficacy was the strongest predictor of intention (β 0.515, p<0.001, large effect), attitude smaller (β 0.206) and perceived norms negligible (β 0.094); intention mediated the path to behavioural willingness.
papers.caveat: Cross-sectional design measuring intention, not actual bystander action at real arrests.
papers.shortTitle: Self-efficacy predicts bystander willingness for CPR
papers.learningGoal: Understand how community self-efficacy shapes bystander CPR willingness so I can strengthen local responder education.

papers.title: Learning from patient-safety-related events in paramedic education: A qualitative study using the SLERT
papers.summary: A Czech qualitative study of 58 undergraduate paramedic students using structured SLERT narratives found patient-safety learning in placements was shaped by role modelling, feedback, emotional processing and reflective meaning-making.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Paramedic students on placements face the same safety pressures here; the findings speak to how Australian educators structure debriefing and safety reflection rather than to clinical practice.
papers.design: Qualitative descriptive study (conventional content analysis)
papers.n: 58 undergraduate paramedic students
papers.finding: Four themes emerged: professional role modelling and feedback, unsafe situations as learning triggers, emotional impact and student vulnerability, and developing patient-safety awareness for future practice.
papers.caveat: Single-country self-reported student narratives, with no outcome follow-up.
papers.shortTitle: Paramedic students learn safety from unsafe events
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my reflective practice so unsafe events and emotional responses on placement deepen my patient-safety awareness.

papers.title: Fatalities in Swedish mountains
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: A Swedish study of mountain rescue fatalities (2018–2023) found drowning and traumatic injuries the leading causes of death among 26 autopsied cases, with half the victims alone when the fatal event occurred.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Alpine and wilderness rescue is a live issue for Australian services; the causes of death and the lone-victim pattern transfer even if the terrain and snowmobile context differ.
papers.design: Descriptive retrospective study (search-and-rescue registry plus autopsy reports)
papers.n: 46 mountain fatalities; autopsy reports for 26
papers.finding: Drowning (n=7) and traumatic injuries (n=7) were the leading causes of death, then suffocation (4), hypothermia (4), disease (3) and intoxication (1); 25 of 26 were male and 13 died alone.
papers.caveat: Autopsy reports were available for only 26 of 46 fatalities, so causes may be incomplete.
papers.shortTitle: Drowning and trauma lead Swedish mountain deaths
papers.learningGoal: Recognise the patterns of preventable death among people recreating alone in remote Australian wilderness settings.

papers.title: Impact of Climatic and Environmental Conditions on Prehospital Emergency Medical Dispatches in Germany: Protocol for an Exploratory, Population-Based Observational Study
papers.summary: A German study protocol plans to link emergency medical dispatch data from two northern metropolitan regions with high-resolution climate data to model temperature–dispatch relationships — no results yet.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Heat already drives Australian dispatch surges and this protocol signals a rigorous European entry into the same question Australian services face now, using dispatch data rather than hospital outcomes.
papers.design: Exploratory retrospective population-based observational protocol (quasi-Poisson, distributed lag nonlinear models)
papers.n: Not reported
papers.finding: Protocol only — will assess nonlinear temperature-response relationships, temporal lags and spatial variation in dispatch volumes across Hanover and Brunswick, comparing high-resolution versus station-based exposure data.
papers.caveat: A protocol with no findings; value depends on data access that isn't yet proven.
papers.shortTitle: Protocol: climate and emergency dispatch volumes
papers.learningGoal: Understand how temperature extremes and environmental conditions shape demand patterns across Australian ambulance dispatch systems.

papers.title: The effects of common emergency call system applications in pre-hospital emergency medical services from a lean management perspective: The case of Ordu province, Turkiye
papers.summary: A retrospective before–after study of 2,346,774 emergency calls in Ordu province, Türkiye found a centralised emergency call centre was associated with a 49% drop in calls per incident and a 36.9% fall in ambulance response time.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A centralised dispatch model in Türkiye — the operational question of call handling, mobilisation and response times is the same here, though a single province's case mix and geography limit direct comparison.
papers.design: Retrospective longitudinal before–after study framed on lean management principles
papers.n: 2,346,774 emergency calls and 721,897 cases over 84 months
papers.finding: Calls per incident fell 49.0% (4.63 to 2.36), ambulance response time fell 36.9% and mobilisation time 23.7%; on-time arrival improved (urban 93.9% to 98.4%, rural 82.2% to 89.2%)
papers.caveat: Before–after design with no adjustment for secular trends or other system changes over eight years
papers.shortTitle: Centralised call centres linked to leaner ambulance operations
papers.learningGoal: Understand how centralised call-taking and dispatch systems shape ambulance response times across urban and rural Australia.

papers.title: Sudden Deaths From Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage and Proximity to Neurosurgical Tertiary Care
papers.summary: A Finnish–New Zealand population cohort of 12,912 patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage found 70.5% of 30-day deaths occurred without neurosurgical unit admission, with higher proportions in districts farther from a neurosurgical centre.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Registry epidemiology from Finland and New Zealand — most SAH deaths happen before neurosurgical care ever starts, which speaks to prehospital recognition and destination decisions rather than any treatment paramedics deliver.
papers.design: Retrospective nationwide cohort from two administrative data collections
papers.n: 12,912 patients with aneurysmal SAH across 41 hospital districts in Finland and New Zealand
papers.finding: 3,819 of 5,418 SAH deaths (70.5%) occurred without neurosurgical unit admission — 70.7% in Finland, 70.1% in New Zealand — and the proportion rose with distance from a neurosurgical centre (age- and sex-adjusted RR 1.07 close-distance, higher farther out)
papers.caveat: Observational administrative data, so distance itself is associated with, not proven to cause, death without admission
papers.shortTitle: Most fatal brain bleeds die before neurosurgery
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my recognition of sudden deterioration suggestive of aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage in rural and remote patients.

papers.title: The Australian Capital Territory breathlessness intervention service (ABIS): a co-designed feasibility study
papers.summary: An Australian co-designed feasibility study of a home-based breathlessness intervention service found 140 completers over 22 months, with 90% reporting improvement in daily activities and 21% reporting they had avoided calling an ambulance for breathlessness.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — An Australian community service rather than an ambulance pathway, but its ambulance-avoidance outcome is directly relevant to how frequent breathlessness callers could be supported elsewhere in the system.
papers.design: Co-designed feasibility study with mixed-methods evaluation
papers.n: 140 patients completing the programme over 22 months
papers.finding: 90% reported improvement on activities of daily living, 70% on 'worst' breathlessness and 68% on mastery; 21% reported avoiding an ambulance call using the strategies they learned
papers.caveat: Single-arm feasibility study without a control group; outcomes were self-reported and the 100-patient 12-month recruitment goal was missed
papers.shortTitle: Breathlessness self-management linked to fewer ambulance calls
papers.learningGoal: Understand how non-pharmacological breathlessness self-management strategies can reduce urgent ambulance demand for chronic respiratory patients.

papers.title: Field Amputation by helicopter emergency service personnel: A cross-sectional survey of clinical practice and experience within air ambulance services in England
papers.summary: A survey of all English air ambulance services found every one could perform prehospital field amputation and four had completed six cases in five years, with a Gigli saw the standard bone instrument and little national standardisation.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Field amputation sits with physician-staffed helicopter services rather than routine road crews in Australia, but the questions it raises — governance, training, equipment, case registries — are the same ones Australian HEMS teams face.
papers.design: Cross-sectional survey of air ambulance services
papers.n: 14 UK helicopter emergency medical services (all England)
papers.finding: All 14 services could provide field amputation; 12 (86%) had a specific clinical practice guideline; 4 services performed 6 cases in five years; a Gigli saw was the most common disarticulation instrument (93%); none used hospital response teams
papers.caveat: Self-reported survey with only six cases nationally in five years, so the clinical practice data are thin
papers.shortTitle: Field amputation: broad capability, little standardisation
papers.learningGoal: Understand how rare prehospital amputation capability is planned and governed in a low-frequency, high-risk setting.

papers.title: Competences of Paramedics in Prehospital Emergency Care: An Umbrella Review
papers.summary: A Finnish-led umbrella review of 20 studies defined the competences paramedics need in out-of-hospital emergency care, organised into five domains: interpersonal and teamwork, cognitive and decision-making, professionalism and ethical, clinical, and situation-specific or high-stress competence.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Finnish-led, but the five competence domains map closely onto Australian paramedic registration standards and the expanding scope of practice debate.
papers.design: Umbrella review (Joanna Briggs Institute methodology, GRADE-CERQual)
papers.n: 8 reviews synthesised from 2,224 screened records
papers.finding: Five competence domains identified: interpersonal and teamwork; cognitive and decision-making; professionalism and ethical; clinical; and competence across certification levels and in special or high-stress situations
papers.caveat: The review stops at describing domains — which educational approaches best build and maintain competence remains unknown
papers.shortTitle: What competence actually means for paramedics
papers.learningGoal: Understand how the five competence domains apply to my scope of practice across routine and high-stress situations.

papers.title: Integrating clinical research into emergency medical services: lessons from the PreMeFen trial
papers.summary: A Norwegian survey of 67 ambulance personnel in the PreMeFen RCT found integrating research into EMS was feasible but demanding: 28% protocol deviations across 338 inclusions, motivation declining over 18 months, and 51% finding study communication excessive — yet 90% would take part in future research.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A Norwegian regional EMS, but the training, motivation and communication lessons apply directly to Australian services running or joining prehospital trials.
papers.design: Cross-sectional survey with linked trial process data
papers.n: 67 of 70 invited ambulance personnel (96% response)
papers.finding: 94 protocol deviations across 338 inclusions (28%), mostly early with missing measurements the commonest cause; motivation fell from median 8 to 7 over 18 months; 51% found communication excessive; 90% willing to participate in future research
papers.caveat: Single regional EMS with self-reported survey data
papers.shortTitle: What running an ambulance trial really takes
papers.learningGoal: Understand the system factors that affect paramedics' sustained engagement and data quality when research is embedded in routine practice.

papers.title: Prehospital Reverse Shock Index multiplied by the Glasgow Coma Scale score (rSIG) as a predictor of urgent interventions in trauma patients: a retrospective cohort study
papers.summary: A Japanese single-centre retrospective cohort tested prehospital rSIG (reverse shock index multiplied by GCS) in 747 trauma patients, finding rSIG below 24.8 was associated with resuscitative interventions (adjusted OR 3.17) and 24-hour transfusion (aOR 4.20) in the validation cohort, but not with surgery, interventional radiology or in-hospital mortality.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — rSIG comes from vital signs and GCS every crew records, so the tool itself travels - but this is one Japanese centre with a derived cutoff and mixed results, not an adopted triage rule.
papers.design: Single-centre retrospective observational cohort with derivation and validation arms
papers.n: 747 trauma patients (505 derivation, 242 validation)
papers.finding: Optimal prehospital rSIG cutoff 24.8; lower rSIG associated with resuscitative interventions (aOR 3.17, 95% CI 1.34-7.50) and blood transfusion within 24 hours (aOR 4.20, 95% CI 1.36-12.95); no significant association with surgery or interventional radiology within 24 hours or with in-hospital mortality
papers.caveat: Single-centre retrospective design with a derived cutoff needing external validation before any clinical use
papers.shortTitle: rSIG cutoff flags trauma patients needing intervention
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the value of prehospital rSIG in recognising trauma patients likely to need urgent resuscitative intervention.

papers.title: Prehospital Trauma Scoring Systems for Discriminating Recorded Secondary Transfer in Multiply Injured Patients: A Comparative Study with Machine Learning
papers.summary: A Turkish EMS record review of 1,194 multiply injured patients compared eight prehospital trauma scores for predicting secondary interhospital transfer, finding CRAMS performed best but only modestly (AUC 0.676), while a random forest model reached AUC 0.836.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Trauma destination and transfer decisions are made by crews everywhere, but the scores discriminated weakly and the better-performing machine-learning model is unvalidated.
papers.design: Retrospective cohort with ROC comparison of eight trauma scores and machine learning
papers.n: 1,194 multiply injured patients (47% secondarily transferred)
papers.finding: CRAMS had the highest score discrimination (AUC 0.676); paediatric age (OR 4.46), elderly age (OR 2.44) and thoracic injury (OR 1.68) were independently associated with transfer; random forest AUC 0.836 versus 0.765 for logistic regression, with calibration compressed toward average risk
papers.caveat: Single-province EMS records, weak score discrimination, and a model needing recalibration and external validation
papers.shortTitle: Prehospital trauma scores poorly predict secondary transfer
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my judgement on when a multiply injured patient will need secondary interhospital transfer.

papers.title: 198. The triage performance of emergency medical dispatch prioritisation compared to prehospital on-scene triage in the Western Cape Province of South Africa
papers.summary: A South African review of 242,576 emergency dispatches found dispatch priority ratings overtriaged 62% and undertriaged 15% of incidents against scene triage, with the highest undertriage in respiratory, diabetic and chest pain calls.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Dispatch triage accuracy shapes every ambulance response, and the undertriage pattern in respiratory and chest pain calls is a warning any dispatch centre should read.
papers.design: Retrospective analysis of computer-aided dispatch records and electronic patient care records
papers.n: 242,576 primary emergency responses
papers.finding: Overtriage 62.28% and undertriage 15.29% against the South African Triage Scale; sensitivity 53.71%, specificity 74.31%; highest undertriage in respiratory complaints (31%), diabetes (30%) and chest pain (29%)
papers.caveat: Single South African dispatch system, compared against scene triage ratings that carry their own error
papers.shortTitle: Dispatch triage overcalls and misses across call types
papers.learningGoal: Understand the limitations of dispatch-based triage in recognising time-critical respiratory, diabetic and chest pain presentations.

papers.title: The Impact of Coordination Between Ambulance Services and Emergency Departments on Healthcare Quality
papers.summary: A narrative review of ambulance-ED coordination evidence found prehospital notification consistently associated with faster diagnosis and reperfusion in stroke and myocardial infarction, structured handover tools with better information transfer, and ambulance diversion with little crowding relief and links to higher mortality in time-sensitive conditions.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Ramping, handover and prenotification are everyday pressure points for Australian crews, but this is a single-author narrative review rather than a systematic one, so treat it as a map of the evidence.
papers.design: Narrative review (SANRA-informed) of offload, handover, prenotification, diversion and governance literature
papers.n: Not reported (PubMed, CINAHL, Embase, Scopus and grey literature)
papers.finding: Prehospital notification associated with faster diagnosis and reperfusion in stroke and myocardial infarction; structured handover tools improved completeness and efficiency; prolonged offload associated with harm and lost ambulance capacity; diversion offered little relief and was linked to higher mortality in time-sensitive conditions
papers.caveat: Narrative review by a single author in a low-profile journal - no systematic search protocol or pooled effect estimates
papers.shortTitle: What the evidence says about ambulance-ED handover
papers.learningGoal: Understand how prehospital notification and structured handover shape patient outcomes during ambulance to emergency department transfers.

papers.title: Comparison of intravenous and intraosseous access performed by paramedic students on two paediatric simulation models: a within-subject simulation study
papers.journal: Journal of Nursing, Social Studies, Public Health and Rehabilitation
papers.summary: A Czech within-subject simulation study had 50 paramedic students attempt paediatric IV on an arm trainer and intraosseous insertion on a high-fidelity manikin, finding IO completed with verified patency in 50 of 50 attempts versus IV in 4 of 50.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — IO access is standard kit across Australian services and paediatric vascular access failures are real, but the students rated the models unrealistic and the authors state nothing can be extrapolated to patients.
papers.design: Within-subject simulation study with fixed task order and a single non-blinded assessor
papers.n: 50 second- and third-year paramedic students
papers.finding: IO insertion with verified patency 50/50 attempts (100%, mean 118.1 s); IV catheterisation 4/50 (8%, mean 288.9 s among successes); 92% of students rated IV more demanding and 88% found the models unrealistic or only partly realistic
papers.caveat: Two different simulator models in fixed order - the authors state the findings describe simulator performance and cannot be extrapolated to clinical practice
papers.shortTitle: Paediatric IO sim success beat IV in students
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my judgement on when to escalate from paediatric intravenous cannulation to intraosseous access in the prehospital setting.

papers.title: Impact of the COVID ‐19 Pandemic on Ambulance Transport for Suspected Bacterial Pneumonia and In‐Hospital Mortality: A Population‐Based ORION Study
papers.summary: A Japanese population registry study of 78,720 patients transported for suspected bacterial pneumonia in Osaka found difficult ambulance transport (four or more hospital selections and 30+ minutes on scene) rose from 2.7% pre-pandemic to 10.3% during COVID-19 and was associated with higher in-hospital mortality (adjusted OR 1.14).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Hospital refusal of ambulances and prolonged transports are live pressures here too, though the Japanese hospital-acceptance system and EMT diagnosis coding differ from Australian arrangements.
papers.design: Retrospective population-based registry study (Osaka ORION), 2018-2023
papers.n: 78,720 patients transported for suspected bacterial pneumonia (65,510 physician-diagnosed)
papers.finding: Difficult transport rose from 2.7% (2018-2019) to 10.3% (2020-2022) and 9.3% (2023); difficult transport associated with higher in-hospital mortality (adjusted OR 1.14, 95% CI 1.03-1.25); transport rates fell from 166.3 to 117.3 per 100,000 residents then returned to 167.0 by 2023
papers.caveat: Japanese registry with EMT-based diagnosis coding and a pandemic-era case mix that shifted alongside the transport changes
papers.shortTitle: Harder ambulance transports, higher pneumonia mortality
papers.learningGoal: Understand how prolonged hospital selection during transport affects outcomes for patients with suspected pneumonia.

papers.title: Built environment and emergency medical services response time in a high-density megacity: multilevel evidence from urban-suburban
papers.summary: A Chinese multilevel regression of 2024 Beijing ambulance dispatch data found denser arterial and local road networks were associated with shorter EMS response times citywide, while denser residential development was linked to slower responses in the central city.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A high-density megacity's built form differs from Australian cities, but the road-density-versus-residential-density signal is useful for response-time planning in our own growth corridors.
papers.design: Retrospective multilevel regression of ambulance dispatch data
papers.n: Not reported (2024 Beijing Emergency Center dispatch data)
papers.finding: Lower residential facility density and denser arterial and local road networks were associated with shorter response times; high residential density was associated with slower responses in central urban areas, while local-road density mattered most in suburbs
papers.caveat: Single megacity with a very different urban form from Australian cities, and associations only — no causal claim
papers.shortTitle: Street layout linked to EMS response times
papers.learningGoal: Understand how urban street layout and residential density shape ambulance response times in Australian cities.

papers.title: Fatal non-avalanche snow burial in Japanese backcountry terrain: a case series of head-first burial in non–tree-well environments
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: A Japanese review of police records across five winters characterised six fatal non-avalanche snow burials in backcountry terrain, all buried head-first with only the lower limbs visible.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — A niche mountain-hazard case series — most useful for alpine and retrieval teams rather than everyday ambulance practice.
papers.design: Retrospective case series (prefectural police record review)
papers.n: 6 fatal cases over 5 years
papers.finding: All six victims were buried head-first in open slopes, terrain depressions or forested terrain (none in tree wells); five were in cardiopulmonary arrest or confirmed dead at recovery, and three had been travelling alone
papers.caveat: Only six cases, all fatal, with clinical detail limited to what police records captured
papers.shortTitle: Head-first snow burial: six Japanese deaths
papers.learningGoal: Recognise terrain features and travel practices that increase the risk of head-first snow burial in backcountry settings.

papers.title: Effect of airway assistant training on intubation time during simulated prehospital airway management: A pilot study
papers.summary: An Australian pilot randomised simulation of 12 paramedic–ICP pairs found a one-hour airway assistant training course cut median intubation time in a continuously regurgitating airway from 102.5 to 53 seconds.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Airway management at intubation is core business for crews across Australian services and the assistant role exists on every two-paramedic response — the open question is whether a 12-person manikin result holds on patients.
papers.design: Pilot randomised simulation study (SALAD manikin)
papers.n: 12 qualified paramedics in two groups of 6, paired with intensive care paramedics
papers.finding: Median intubation time 53 s (IQR 19) trained vs 102.5 s (IQR 36) untrained, p = 0.009, very large effect size (Cohen's d = 1.86); no oesophageal intubations in either group
papers.caveat: Pilot simulation with 12 participants — no patient outcomes, and the authors call for larger studies
papers.shortTitle: Airway assistant training halved sim intubation time
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my ability to assist effectively during prehospital intubation in soiled or regurgitating airways.

papers.title: On-Scene Time-Dependent Probabilities of Return of Spontaneous Circulation and Favorable Neurological Outcome in Cases of Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest with an Initial Shockable Rhythm: A Retrospective Study Using the National Utstein Data in Japan
papers.summary: A Japanese national Utstein cohort of 22,383 adults with shockable cardiogenic OHCA found the probability of subsequent on-scene ROSC fell from 6.97% at 10 minutes to 0.50% at 20 minutes of resuscitation, with favourable neurological outcome in 50.0% of under-75s achieving on-scene ROSC at or after 10 minutes.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Shockable-rhythm resuscitation duration and transport decisions are made by paramedics across Australia, and this is a 22,383-patient national registry over six years.
papers.design: Retrospective nationwide Utstein descriptive cohort, 2017–2022
papers.n: 22,383 adults with cardiogenic OHCA and an initial shockable rhythm
papers.finding: Probability of subsequent on-scene ROSC 6.97% at 10 min and 0.50% at 20 min after EMS contact; favourable neurological outcome (CPC 1–2 at 1 month) in 50.0% of patients <75 and 20.5% of those ≥75 with on-scene ROSC at or after 10 min
papers.caveat: Descriptive Japanese EMS data — no causal claims, and the authors state it does not establish age-based criteria for prolonged resuscitation or transport
papers.shortTitle: Numbers for when on-scene ROSC stops happening
papers.learningGoal: Weigh when ongoing on-scene resuscitation in shockable cardiac arrest remains worthwhile against early transport decisions.

papers.title: Modelled Response Times for Police and Fire Brigade Co-Dispatch to Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Geospatial Simulation Study in Vorarlberg, Austria
papers.summary: An Austrian geospatial simulation of 500 modelled OHCA locations found police and volunteer fire brigade co-dispatch cut modelled median first-unit response time from 9.81 to 5.41 minutes and lifted 10-minute coverage from 51.1% to 94.6%.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A modelled European system with volunteer fire stations, but first-responder co-response to cardiac arrest is a live resourcing question for Australian services too.
papers.design: Geospatial routing simulation
papers.n: 500 modelled OHCA locations served by 18 EMS, 28 police and 121 volunteer fire stations
papers.finding: Median first-unit response 9.81 min with EMS alone vs 5.45 min with police added, 7.36 min with fire added, 5.41 min with triple dispatch (paired median gain 4.34 min); locations reached within 10 min rose from 51.1% to 94.6%
papers.caveat: Purely modelled — fixed stations, assumed turnout times, continuous availability assumed, and the authors say operational validation is required
papers.shortTitle: Co-dispatch modelled to cut OHCA response times
papers.learningGoal: Understand how co-dispatching first responders could reduce time to first unit in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Workplace Violence Exposure and Burnout Among Fire-Service-Based Paramedics in South Korea: The Indirect Association Through Post-Traumatic Stress Symptoms and the Moderating Roles of Social Support and Resilience
papers.summary: A South Korean cross-sectional study of 210 fire-service paramedics found workplace violence exposure was associated with burnout indirectly through post-traumatic stress symptoms, with social support weakening that pathway.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — South Korean fire-service paramedics, but violence exposure, PTSD symptoms and burnout are occupational realities for paramedics everywhere, and social support is something services can build.
papers.design: Cross-sectional moderated mediation survey
papers.n: 210 fire-service-based paramedics in Busan
papers.finding: Workplace violence exposure associated with burnout indirectly through post-traumatic stress symptoms; social support moderated the violence–PTSS (p = 0.002) and violence–burnout (p = 0.015) associations; resilience findings did not survive correction
papers.caveat: Cross-sectional self-report, and some social-support findings depended on excluding one influential observation
papers.shortTitle: Social support buffers the violence-to-burnout pathway
papers.learningGoal: Understand how social support buffers the impact of workplace violence on my wellbeing and burnout risk.

papers.title: Associations of Secondary Traumatic Stress and Emotional Labor with Suicidal Ideation Among Emergency Dispatch Personnel in South Korea: A Cross-Sectional Moderated Mediation Analysis
papers.summary: A South Korean survey of 211 emergency dispatch personnel found secondary traumatic stress and depression were associated with suicidal ideation, with the indirect pathway through depression weakening as social support rose.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Dispatchers sit upstream of every ambulance response, and the secondary-trauma and social-support findings speak to Australian ambulance communications centres too.
papers.design: Cross-sectional moderated mediation survey
papers.n: 211 fire-service emergency dispatch personnel in Busan and Gyeongnam
papers.finding: Conditional indirect association of secondary traumatic stress with suicidal ideation through depression fell from 0.191 at low social support to 0.013 at high; emotional labour pathways held only at low and mean support
papers.caveat: Cross-sectional, and key suicidal-ideation interaction terms were not significant in a Tobit sensitivity analysis
papers.shortTitle: Dispatch stress, depression and suicidal ideation linked
papers.learningGoal: Understand how social support buffers secondary traumatic stress and depression in my emergency communication workforce.

papers.title: Apparent temperature, heat waves, and unintentional injury-related emergency medical service calls: A case-crossover study
papers.summary: A Shanghai case-crossover study of 170,538 unintentional injury-related EMS calls found extreme apparent temperature (42.5 °C vs −2.9 °C) was associated with 21% higher odds of injury calls, peaking at 80% higher for traffic injuries.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Shanghai demand data, but heat-driven injury call surges map straight onto Australian summers and the dispatch resourcing that comes with them.
papers.design: Time-stratified case-crossover with distributed lag models
papers.n: 170,538 unintentional injury-related EMS calls, July 2021 – June 2025
papers.finding: Cumulative OR 1.21 (95% CI 1.12–1.31) comparing the 99th percentile apparent temperature (42.5 °C) with the exposure minimum; traffic injuries OR 1.80 (95% CI 1.56–2.07); adults 18–64 OR 1.38; heat waves OR 1.07
papers.caveat: Single Shanghai district, and comparisons across heat-wave definitions and exposure windows were exploratory
papers.shortTitle: Hot days, more injury calls to ambulance services
papers.learningGoal: Understand how extreme heat drives demand surges and injury risk in Australian ambulance operations.

papers.title: The global research landscape of emergency medical services in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
papers.summary: A US-led bibliometric analysis of 3,005 Web of Science records from 1972–2026 mapped EMS-focused OHCA research, showing output above 200 papers a year since 2022 and registry-centred international collaboration.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A map of the research field rather than a clinical result — background on where EMS-OHCA evidence comes from and how much of it flows through the big registries.
papers.design: Retrospective bibliometric analysis (Web of Science, VOSviewer)
papers.n: 3,005 records, 1972 – June 2026
papers.finding: Annual output peaked at 244 publications in 2021 and stayed above 200 from 2022–2025; Resuscitation published 23.1% of records; the US led with 34.0%, then Japan 12.5% and Canada 9.4%
papers.caveat: Bibliometrics only — publication counts and co-citations, no clinical findings
papers.shortTitle: Mapping 50 years of EMS cardiac arrest research
papers.learningGoal: Understand how international registry-based collaboration shapes the prehospital cardiac arrest evidence I apply in practice.

papers.title: Prehospital Advanced Airway Management in Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Cohort Study Using Time-Dependent Propensity Score Sequential Matching
papers.summary: A Japanese nationwide registry cohort of 7,217 adults with traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest found successful prehospital advanced airway management was not significantly associated with better 30-day survival or neurological outcome when resuscitation-time bias was corrected.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Supraglottic airways are standard Australian cardiac arrest care and intubation is an advanced-tier skill in most services, so the question is squarely ours; the physician-free Japanese EMS model resembles ours more than Europe's.
papers.design: Nationwide retrospective registry cohort with time-dependent propensity score sequential matching
papers.n: 7,217 adults with traumatic OHCA (2,653 received advanced airway management)
papers.finding: Thirty-day survival 1.8% with advanced airway vs 1.4% matched controls (corrected RD 0.6%, 95% CI −0.1 to 1.2); favourable neurological outcome 0.2% vs 0.4% (corrected RD −0.2%, 95% CI −0.6 to 0.1) — no significant timing-dependent association
papers.caveat: Observational design with extremely low event rates, so even a real effect could hide in the confidence intervals
papers.shortTitle: Advanced airway not linked to traumatic arrest survival
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the value of advanced airway management during traumatic cardiac arrest against prioritising early ventilation and circulation.

papers.title: Prehospital recognition and differentiation of seizure presentations by paramedics and ambulance nurses: A scoping review
papers.summary: An Australian scoping review of 18 studies found paramedic recognition of seizure presentations remains suboptimal, with sensitivity of 54.0–58.5% and non-recognition of non-convulsive seizures reaching 53.0–81.4%.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Diagnostic accuracy of seizure recognition is a crew-level problem everywhere, and the review covers paramedic practice directly comparable to Australian scope.
papers.design: Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) of 18 studies across five databases
papers.n: 18 studies (16 paramedic, 2 ambulance nurse) from 1,264 citations
papers.finding: Sensitivity 54.0–58.5% and specificity 95.9–96.6% against variable reference standards; recognition rates 56.8–89.7%; non-convulsive seizures missed in 53.0–81.4% of cases
papers.caveat: Included studies used variable reference standards and EMS workforce configurations, limiting pooled interpretation
papers.shortTitle: Paramedics miss many non-convulsive seizures
papers.learningGoal: Recognise non-convulsive seizure presentations in the field to reduce missed diagnoses.

papers.title: Dispatch suspicion of sepsis and time from emergency department arrival to antibiotic administration: a Norwegian registry study
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: A Norwegian registry study of 527 sepsis admissions found dispatch suspicion of sepsis was associated with a 31-minute shorter adjusted time from ED arrival to antibiotic administration.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Dispatch triage criteria and sepsis recognition are core ambulance functions in Australia, and the Nordic dispatch model is close to ours.
papers.design: Retrospective registry-based cohort linking prehospital and hospital records
papers.n: 527 sepsis admissions (371 with emergency dispatch contact; 31 classified as suspected sepsis at dispatch)
papers.finding: Dispatch suspicion of sepsis was associated with a 31-minute shorter adjusted time to antibiotics (95% CI −59.9 to −1.8 min)
papers.caveat: Only 31 patients carried the sepsis dispatch flag, so the estimate rests on a small subgroup
papers.shortTitle: Sepsis suspicion at dispatch, earlier antibiotics
papers.learningGoal: Recognise how early prehospital suspicion of sepsis can accelerate antibiotic administration for deteriorating patients.

papers.title: Frequent Callers to Emergency Medical Services: an observational cohort study from Region Zealand, Denmark (2018-2025)
papers.summary: A Danish observational cohort of 443,977 emergency calls found 3.0% of callers (6,415 people) generated 19.9% of all calls, with post-threshold frequent callers seeing more telephone resolution (23.8%) and non-conveyance (27.4%).
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Frequent-caller patterns and dispatch load are universal ambulance problems, and the Danish single-tier system maps well onto Australian operations.
papers.design: Observational cohort of emergency medical dispatch centre calls, 2018–2025
papers.n: 214,091 individuals making 443,977 calls in Region Zealand, Denmark
papers.finding: Frequent callers (5+ calls in 12 months) were 3.0% of callers but 19.9% of calls; alcohol/intoxication/overdose and suicidal presentations were top contact causes only in the highest-volume post-threshold groups
papers.caveat: Single-region data and a dispatch-centre definition of frequent calling that may not match other systems' operational definitions
papers.shortTitle: 3% of callers drive a fifth of all calls
papers.learningGoal: Understand the system factors that drive frequent calling to ambulance services and how coordinated responses reduce demand.

papers.title: Cycle-to-Cycle Prediction of Return of Spontaneous Circulation Using End-Tidal Carbon Dioxide Dynamics in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
papers.summary: A Taiwanese retrospective multicentre study of 1,480 patients with OHCA built a two-layer LSTM model on sequential EtCO2 that predicted ROSC well at event level (AUROC 0.876) but only 0.685 per two-minute cycle.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — EtCO2 monitoring is routine on Australian cardiac arrests, but this is a retrospective modelling study needing prospective, real-time validation before it guides cycle decisions on the road.
papers.design: Multicentre retrospective study with LSTM prediction model, internally validated by 10-fold cross-validation
papers.n: 1,651 EtCO2 sequences from 1,480 adults with OHCA (583 ROSC events)
papers.finding: Event-level AUROC 0.876 (Brier 0.140); cycle-level AUROC 0.685 across 17,029 two-minute prediction points, with systematic overestimation of ROSC probability (Brier 0.285)
papers.caveat: Retrospective, single-country dataset with internal validation only and poor cycle-level calibration
papers.shortTitle: EtCO2 trends predict ROSC cycle by cycle
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the value of EtCO2 trend monitoring for anticipating return of spontaneous circulation during resuscitation.

papers.title: A national cross-sectional analysis of regional and rural-urban variation in emergency medical services naloxone administration for suspected opioid overdose
papers.journal: Journal of Substance Use and Addiction Treatment
papers.summary: A US cross-sectional analysis of 110,261 EMS activations for suspected opioid overdose found documented naloxone administration in 33.9%, with regional variation (South aOR 2.10 vs Northeast) that persisted while the rural-urban difference attenuated to null after clinical adjustment.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Naloxone is carried by every Australian ambulance service, and the finding is about how documented practice varies with case mix rather than a foreign service model.
papers.design: National cross-sectional analysis of the 2025 NEMSIS public-release dataset with multivariable logistic regression
papers.n: 110,261 EMS activations with suspected opioid involvement (37,412 naloxone administrations)
papers.finding: Adjusted odds of EMS naloxone administration were higher in the South (aOR 2.10, 95% CI 2.01–2.18), Midwest (aOR 1.92) and West (aOR 1.31) versus the Northeast; rural-versus-urban odds were null after clinical adjustment (aOR 1.01, 95% CI 0.94–1.09)
papers.caveat: Administrative documentation of naloxone as a surveillance marker, not a clinical endpoint — variation may reflect documentation and case-mix differences
papers.shortTitle: US naloxone use varies by region, not rurality
papers.learningGoal: Understand how regional and rural factors shape naloxone use and documentation in suspected opioid overdose care.

papers.title: Toward a Definition and Differentiation of Secondary Traumatic Stress, Vicarious Trauma, Post-Traumatic Stress, and Compassion Fatigue in Relation to First Responders: An Integrative Literature Review
papers.summary: A French integrative review of 76 studies on first responders (including paramedics) found the concepts of secondary traumatic stress, vicarious trauma, compassion fatigue and PTSD overlap symptomatically, with organisational constraints playing a central role in traumatic responses.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Workforce psychological injury is a universal ambulance problem, and the review's emphasis on organisational drivers rather than individual resilience speaks directly to Australian services.
papers.design: Integrative literature review of 76 studies across six databases to January 2026
papers.n: 76 studies of adult first responders (firefighters, police, paramedics, ambulance workers)
papers.finding: Conceptual overlap between secondary traumatic stress, vicarious trauma, compassion fatigue and PTSD is maintained by symptomatic overlap and measurement tools designed for other professions; organisational constraints emerged as central to trauma emergence
papers.caveat: Conceptual synthesis with no intervention data, and heterogeneous included professions
papers.shortTitle: Untangling trauma terms for first responders
